query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a thin, dense, and adherent Al2O3-based ceramic coating on as‐cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will significantly improve its high-temperature oxidation resistance without compromising its inherent ductility and yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Apply a ≤10 μm thick Al2O3-based ceramic coating using a high-temperature PVD or CVD process at approximately 800–900 °C under moderate vacuum.
generation.conditions: Exposure to an oxidizing atmosphere (air) at 1000 °C for up to 100 hours with tensile loading at strain rates between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, dense oxide barrier layer formed on the surface that minimizes oxygen diffusion into the underlying bulk alloy.
generation.mechanism: The Al2O3 coating serves as a physical barrier that impedes oxygen ingress at high temperature, thereby protecting the alloy’s surface from oxidation without altering its bulk microstructure or mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated HfNbTaTiZr, the coated alloy will exhibit reduced oxide scale formation and maintain its advantageous mechanical properties (ductility and yield strength) at high temperatures.
generation.baseline: Untreated as-cast HfNbTaTiZr, which shows significant oxidation under high-temperature exposure, leading to performance degradation.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected under continuous exposure in air at 1000 °C for periods up to 100 hours and under tensile loads applied at strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.uncertainty: The long-term coating adhesion and its behavior under cyclic thermal loading remain uncertain; the precise impact of the coating process on near-surface microstructure may also vary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr specimens: one set with the applied ≤10 μm Al2O3 coating via PVD/CVD and one set left untreated. Expose both sets to air at 1000 °C under identical conditions for 100 hours while applying a tensile load at a strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Post-exposure, evaluate surface oxidation and mechanical performance.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and morphology via microscopy and surface analysis (e.g., SEM, EDS)
Room temperature tensile ductility and yield strength
High-temperature mechanical performance (e.g., yield strength at 1000 °C)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxide scale growth and/or if their mechanical properties (ductility and yield strength) deteriorate relative to the untreated controls, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Abstract In this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi 2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M 5 Si 3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature. decision.trend: For equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr (often labeled Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20), early work (PMC5578249) used vacuum arc melting and hot isostatic pressing but did not address oxidation resistance, focusing instead on tensile and creep properties at high temperature and finding significant brittleness at room temperature. Another approach (PMC7513042) improved high-temperature mechanical performance of a refractory high-entropy alloy while aiming to maintain oxidation resistance by adding reinforcement particles through powder metallurgy. However, these studies did not resolve the core challenge of preventing oxygen ingress in as-cast HfNbTaTiZr without altering the bulk composition or compromising its mechanical benefits.
decision.unsolved: Despite promising mechanical performance at 1000 °C, the poor oxygen resistance of as-cast HfNbTaTiZr remains a key barrier to practical high-temperature service. Previous investigations in this material class have emphasized mechanical properties optimization but have not sufficiently addressed surface protection against oxidation without alloy re-design.
decision.lever: Deposit an oxidation-resistant ceramic coating (e.g., Al2O3- or Y2O3-based) via a high-temperature PVD or CVD route at 800–900 °C and moderate vacuum, targeting a dense, adherent layer of ≤10 μm thickness to protect against oxygen ingress in air for up to 100 hours under tensile loading at 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹ and up to 1000 °C.
decision.why: Surface engineering via a thin, stable oxide coating is a single, direct intervention that can shield HfNbTaTiZr from high-temperature oxygen infiltration, maintaining the bulk alloy’s favorable mechanical strength and ductility. Prior high-entropy alloy research (e.g., in PMC7513042) demonstrated that controlling surface reactions can preserve oxidation resistance without sacrificing mechanical performance. A controlled falsification experiment would compare coated versus uncoated specimens in a 1000 °C oxidative environment under tensile loading at 10⁻³ s⁻¹ for up to 100 hours, quantifying oxide scale thickness, oxidation kinetics, and mechanical properties to verify the coating’s effectiveness.
